Section 1

Executive Summary

Over the period from January 2023 to March 2026, plant Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) averaged 66.5%, against a target of 85%. Performance (82.1%), actual machine output rate relative to its ideal rate while running, is the larger part of the shortfall; Availability (85.2%), total machine running time relative to planned production time, is the smaller. Note that Quality is excluded from this report. We assumed a rate of 95% for purposes of calculating OEE.

Plant OEE, Availability, and Performance, Actual vs. Target

The single largest driver of the gap between today's 66.5% OEE and the 85% target is the underperformance of the shop's oldest machines. The 3 aging machines (over nine years old), MCH-011, MCH-007, MCH-012, run at 59% OEE against 69% for the rest of the fleet, about 10 points lower. Their Availability is roughly 8 points below the newer machines (79% versus 87%), because they stop and alarm more often, and their Performance is about 4 points lower (79% versus 83%), because their cycle time is slowed by worn spindles, dated controls and more conservative feeds and speeds. Although they are only 3 of 12 machines, they carry about 38% of the total margin opportunity shown below.

Annual Contribution Margin Opportunity at 85% Target OEE

Reaching the 85% target OEE (implying Availability and Performance of 95%) is worth an estimated $1.3M per year in additional contribution margin ($670K from Availability and $669K from Performance). Closing that gap between actual and target requires execution across a handful of levers, as detailed in Section 6. The two that carry most of the value are capital decisions on the oldest machines: a spindle rebuild and control retrofit, and a reliability review of whether to rebuild or replace them.

Section 2

Machine-level OEE Breakdown

Across all machines, OEE ranges from 55% to 75%. CNC lathes consistently have higher OEE than the vertical and horizontal mills. This pattern is due to the mills being older machines that are most frequently in need of routine maintenance, and that also take the most complex work, and so lose more time to stoppages and generally run slower. The lathes are newer and run simpler jobs. As mentioned, the three aging machines (>9 years old), MCH-011, MCH-007, MCH-012, have the lowest OEE among the fleet.

OEE by Machine

The OEE by machine type holds steady across the period, with no noticeable increases or decreases over time.

OEE Trend by Machine Type

The chart below shows each machine type's planned production time split into three parts: time spent productive (running at target speed), time lost to downtime (an Availability loss), and time lost to slow cycle times (a Performance loss). The productive share of time for each machine type holds fairly steady from month to month.

Section 3

Deep Dive: Availability

The Pareto below shows the shop's unplanned downtime by failure mode over the full period (Jan 2023-Mar 2026). Tooling and mechanical issues each caused about 800 hours of unplanned downtime, and together make up 69% of unplanned repair hours.

Unplanned Downtime by Failure Code

Downtime is not spread evenly through the day. Across the full observation window (Jan 2023-Mar 2026), unplanned stoppages concentrate at the beginning of shifts before steadying across the middle and end of the shifts. As seen in the chart below, during the first 45 minutes of each shift, unplanned stoppages run about 1.2x the mid-shift rate: 1.3x on Shift A and 1.1x on Shift B. A standardised shift-start routine, including a documented warm-up sequence and first-piece check written into the opening of every shift, addresses this window; as detailed in Section 6, it represents a potential contribution margin uplift of about $3K per year.

Unplanned Stoppages by Time Into Shift

Analyzing setup time by operator, we find that most machinists cluster near the cohort median of 27 minutes per job, with just a modest spread across most of the operators. Three of them, OPR-012, OPR-009, OPR-004, sit consistently above the rest at about 1.3x the median, roughly 8 minutes longer on every job they run. There is a potential opportunity for targeted coaching and setup-standardisation to recover Availability at no capital cost.

Median Setup Hours by Operator

Shop-wide on-time calendar PM completion is 72% and uneven, with MCH-007 at only 62%. The repair-interval services were completed before the failure on 97% of occasions: 20 unplanned failures over the period came after the machine's repair-interval had been reached and before a service was carried out. The failures that came after the interval was reached took about 73 hours a year of unplanned repair more than repair-interval services would have taken at each machine's average. And while a machine was overdue on calendar PM, it spent about 45 hours a year in an alarm state above what it spends when its calendar PM is current.

On-Time Maintenance by Machine: Calendar PM and Interval Service
Average downtime per event: calendar PM 4.0 hours, interval service 5.4 hours, unplanned repair 16.0 hours.
Section 4

Deep Dive: Performance

Performance across the shop averaged 82.1% against the 95% target. Unlike Availability, where the losses trace to events (breakdowns, alarms, shift starts and setups), the Performance loss is a steady level that each machine holds from day to day. As seen in the chart below, every machine's daily Performance sits in a narrow band around its own median: the typical machine moves 3 points from one day to the next, while the gap between the best and worst machine is 14 points.

Daily Performance by Machine, Ordered by Age

Performance is closely tied to machine age. Older machines hold a slower cycle through worn spindles, dated controls, and more conservative feeds and speeds. As seen in the chart below, the relationship is strong: across the shop, Performance falls about 1.0 percentage points for every year of machine age (r = -0.78), and machine type accounts for part of what age does not: at the same age, the lathes run about 2 points above the mills.

Performance vs. Machine Age
One point per machine. Fitted line: -1.0 Performance points per year of age, r = -0.78, R² = 0.60.

If Performance were impacted by how the machines are run, it would vary with who is running them and when. As seen in the two panels below, it does not. For each machine, Shift A and Shift B run within 0.1 points of each other, and the spread across the operators who run the same machine is about 1 point (at most 1.4), inside the day-to-day noise of the machine itself. The same machine runs at the same rate whoever is at the controls. This is the opposite of what Section 3 found for Availability, where the shift-start window, PM status and setup discipline each move the figure, and it rules out training and coaching as Performance levers.

Performance Within Machine, by Shift and by Operator
Machines ordered by age. Operators with 50 or more running intervals on the machine, joined through the HR master.

As seen in the Pareto below, Performance losses are carried across the fleet. The two machines that lose the most hours, MCH-006 and MCH-008, are not aging assets: both run about 17 points below target, close to the gap on the aging machines MCH-011 and MCH-007, but they run more hours because their Availability is higher. MCH-012, an aging machine, is among the four machines that lose the fewest hours: while its gap is 11 points, it runs fewer hours due to low Availability. The 3 aging machines carry 33% of the total Performance loss by contribution margin.

Annual Performance Loss by Machine: Hours and Contribution Margin
Bars: running hours lost against the 95% Performance target. Labels: hours, and the Performance margin Section 5 attributes to the machine, which totals $669K.
Section 5

Margin Uplift Opportunity Detail

The OEE misses detailed above translate directly into lost contribution margin, the incremental profit on each productive machine hour (revenue net of variable cost). Valued at each machine type's contribution margin (CNC Lathes $95/hr, Vertical Mills $125/hr, Horizontal Mills $145/hr), reaching the 85% target is worth an estimated $1.3 million per year. This opportunity is split between Availability ($670K per year), meaning less machine downtime and faster changeovers, and Performance ($669K per year), meaning running machines nearer ideal speed.

Within Availability, unplanned reactive repairs run about $93K per year (719 hours), a small part of the total, since the interval services pre-empt most failures. The balance is idle, setup and changeover time, where the operator setup-time gap is one opportunity. Within Performance, the loss is a steady level on each machine, highest on the oldest machines as detailed above.

Annual Contribution Margin Uplift Opportunity at 85% OEE, by Machine
Section 6

Recommended Actions

The findings resolve into six actions, ranked below by the annual impact each one carries. The list spans both low- and high-capital moves, from routine and coaching changes that cost little to the capital decisions on the oldest assets. Two capital actions on the oldest machines carry 93% of the total; the other four are low-cost and small. The estimates are drawn from the same data and contribution-margin assumptions used throughout this report.

ActionSupporting Finding Est. Annual ImpactCapital Required
Spindle rebuild and control retrofit on the oldest machinesPerformance falls about 1.0 points per year of machine age$222KHigh
Reliability review, rebuild versus replace, for MCH-011, MCH-007Oldest assets carry the most unplanned downtime (P1)$178KHigh
Tooling program: vendor consolidation and tool-life trackingTooling and mechanical are level as the largest unplanned categories, 35% and 34% of unplanned hours$13KLow
Setup standardisation coaching for OPR-012, OPR-009, OPR-004Setups at 1.3x the cohort median (P4)$10KNone
Standardised shift-start warm-up and first-piece routine on both shiftsStoppages run 1.2x higher in a shift's first 45 minutes (P2)$3KNone
PM catch-up and compliance enforcementWithin-machine PM-overdue to alarm-rate linkage (P3)$3KMinimal
